article.overview: A lunar agriculture demonstrator is a payload designed to show whether plants can germinate, grow and be harvested under lunar conditions, as a step towards food production for future Moon bases. No flown demonstrator in the sources reviewed has shown a plant completing a full growth cycle on the Moon. The closest flown example is the Chinese Chang'e-4 mini-biosphere of 2019, in which cotton seeds sprouted before the plants died during the first lunar night [2][3]. Apollo 14 carried tree seeds to lunar orbit, but they were not grown on the Moon [4]. Laboratory studies using Apollo lunar regolith show that seeds can germinate in lunar soil, although growth is slower and more stressed than in a simulant [1]. This article keeps flown examples, laboratory evidence and design concepts separate.
article.description: A lunar agriculture demonstrator would carry plant seeds, and often other organisms, to the Moon in a sealed or controlled enclosure and monitor their development under real surface conditions. Simple versions are small sealed biological canisters that test whether germination and survival are possible through a lunar day and night. More ambitious concepts are greenhouse modules that test crop cultivation using lunar regolith, with water, air and nutrients supplied from a life-support system [5][6]. Typical measurements include germination rate, growth, plant health, the temperature and gas conditions inside the enclosure, and the chemistry of the growth medium. Lunar regolith is the fine, broken material covering the Moon's surface. Studies of Apollo samples linked plant stress to chemical differences between regolith and the simulants normally used on Earth, and the authors suspect chemical differences such as the oxidation state of iron [1].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose is to establish whether food plants and other organisms can be grown in the lunar environment, and under what conditions. Potential applications include supplementing crew food, producing fibre and oil, and using plants within a closed loop that exchanges oxygen, carbon dioxide and water with the crew. Chang'e-4 designers suggested that cotton could provide fabric, potato and rockcress could provide food, and rapeseed could yield oil, but these uses were described as hypothetical [3]. The ESA MELiSSA greenhouse concept would link crop production to a closed life-support loop, with a stated goal of decreasing resupply launch mass [5][6].
article.operating_principle: Plants grow by photosynthesis, which requires light, water, carbon dioxide and nutrients, so a lunar demonstrator must supply each of these inside a sealed or pressurised enclosure, because the Moon has no atmosphere to retain air. The enclosure must also keep organisms warm enough during the lunar night, which is why the Chang'e-4 canister included a heating system and two cameras to observe growth [2][3]. In a closed-loop design the principle extends further: plants take up carbon dioxide and water, release oxygen, and return harvested crops and inedible biomass to the loop, as envisaged for the GreenMOSS greenhouse [6]. Laboratory studies test the growth medium separately: seeds are sown in regolith and in a reference simulant, and germination, root and shoot growth, and gene expression are compared [1].
article.scientific_importance: Lunar agriculture matters because any long-duration crewed presence on the Moon would need either to carry all of its food from Earth or to produce part of it locally. Resupply from Earth is costly, and reducing it is a stated aim of the MELiSSA greenhouse concept [5][6]. The Apollo regolith study showed that plants can germinate in lunar soil at rates close to those in a simulant, but that growth is impaired and stress-related genes are switched on in plants grown in every Apollo soil tested [1]. The main scientific problem is therefore not only whether seeds sprout but how regolith chemistry and structure limit growth, and whether treatment or conditioning is needed [1]. The Chang'e-4 experiment is the only flown experiment in the sources reviewed that reported germination on the Moon, and its result is a single observation under one thermal history [2][3].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a lunar agriculture demonstrator, and the sources reviewed do not describe a standard design. The examples below differ in purpose and status: one flown canister, one flown seed-carriage experiment, one Earth-based laboratory study using Apollo samples, and one design study. They must not be compared as if they were the same hardware. Values are given only where a source reports them, and unverified figures are marked as such.

examples.name: Chang'e-4 Lunar Micro Ecosystem
examples.description: Type: flown lunar biology experiment (2019). The Chang'e-4 lander reached the lunar far side on 3 January 2019 [3]. It carried a sealed mini-biosphere designed by Chongqing University. Secondary coverage describes it as an 18 cm long canister of about 2.6 kg, while another report describes it as a roughly six-pound canister; neither figure was verified against a primary source. Reported contents were cotton, potato, rapeseed and Arabidopsis seeds, yeast and fruit-fly eggs, together with water, soil, air, two cameras and a heating system [2][3]. Only the cotton seeds were reported to sprout [2], although other coverage suggests rapeseed and potato may also have sprouted, so this is not settled [3]. The team reported that the canister reached –62 °F (about –52 °C) [2]. The sprouts died after about 213 hours, when the lunar night began and the power went out, because the experiment had no battery [2].
examples.mass_and_size_notes: Secondary coverage reports an 18 cm long canister and about 2.6 kg, and another report describes a roughly six-pound canister. Not verified against a primary source; recorded as null.
examples.power_notes: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed; the canister had a heating system and, per one report, no battery.

examples.name: Apollo 14 Moon tree seeds
examples.description: Type: flown seed-carriage experiment (1971). Apollo 14 launched on 31 January 1971. Command module pilot Stuart Roosa carried a seed set in the command module and orbited the Moon while Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell landed [4]. NASA reports 'possibly 2,000 or more seeds' and, in another passage, 'hundreds of tree seeds', of five species: loblolly pine, sycamore, sweetgum, redwood and Douglas fir [4]. The seeds were not grown on the Moon. NASA reports that the seed bags burst open during post-flight decontamination, leaving viability in doubt, and that most seedlings were later given to state forestry organisations around the 1975–1976 bicentennial period [4]. This example is included as a historical case of plant material carried to lunar orbit; it is not a growth demonstrator.

examples.name: Apollo lunar regolith plant-growth study (laboratory)
examples.type: Earth-based laboratory study using Apollo samples (not flown)
examples.description: Type: Earth-based laboratory study using Apollo samples (not flown). Paul, Elardo and Ferl grew Arabidopsis thaliana in regolith from Apollo 11, 12 and 17 samples and in the JSC-1A simulant [1]. Germination was close to 100% in all Apollo regolith sources and indistinguishable from the simulant, but seedlings grown in lunar soil had more stunted roots, slower growth, smaller leaf canopies and stress pigmentation [1]. Transcriptomic analysis showed stress-related gene expression associated with salt, metal and reactive oxygen species [1]. The Apollo 11 regolith, considered the most mature of the three soils, caused the most stress, and the Apollo 17 regolith the least [1]. The authors suggest that repeated cultivation to condition the soil, or cycling water through the regolith, may be needed for good growth [1]. Sample masses and exact growth statistics were not verified from full text.

examples.name: MELiSSA GreenMOSS lunar greenhouse
examples.type: Proposed design study (not built or flown)
examples.description: Type: proposed design study (not built or flown). The GreenMOSS preliminary design study, carried out by DLR and partners under ESA's MELiSSA framework, considered a lunar surface greenhouse module [6]. The chosen design uses an inflatable outer shell around a rigid inner core, with a cultivation area reported as over 650 m² and a projected yield of more than 4,100 kg of edible dry mass over the mission [6]. ESA sets a requirement that the greenhouse operate for at least 24 lunar sidereal days, about 655 Earth days [5][6]. These are design targets, not measured performance. ESA's MELiSSA page states that priority has so far been given to a fully functional closed-loop life-support system on the ground [5]. No flight date has been identified in the sources reviewed.
examples.projected_edible_dry_mass_kg: more than 4100 (design target, not a measurement)
examples.operating_duration_requirement: at least 24 lunar sidereal days (about 655 Earth days); requirement as reported

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No verified dimension applies to a lunar agriculture demonstrator as a class. The Chang'e-4 canister size is reported only in secondary coverage and is unverified. The GreenMOSS cultivation area is a design target, not a measured dimension.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: No verified mass applies to a lunar agriculture demonstrator as a class. The Chang'e-4 canister mass is reported only in secondary coverage (about 2.6 kg in one summary, a roughly six-pound canister in another) and is unverified.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed for any example. The Chang'e-4 canister had a heating system; its power source is described only as having run out during the lunar night.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar agriculture payload would face vacuum, large surface temperature swings between lunar day and night, ionising radiation, micrometeoroid exposure and dust. The Chang'e-4 canister's reported internal low of –62 °F (about –52 °C), and the plants' death when the lunar night began, show that thermal control through the night is the most immediate constraint [2]. Plants also need light and a controlled supply of water, gas and nutrients, and regolith may need conditioning before it supports growth [1]. The GreenMOSS concept sets an operating target of at least 24 lunar sidereal days, about 655 Earth days, which implies lifetime, power and life-support requirements far beyond a single lunar day [5][6]. Specific radiation, dust and pressure tolerance values are not publicly specified for any example reviewed.
article.limitations: The evidence base is thin. Only one flown experiment in the sources reviewed reported germination on the Moon, and its plants died after about 213 hours [2]. Reports on which seeds sprouted in the Chang'e-4 canister conflict [2][3]. The Apollo 14 seeds were not grown on the Moon [4]. The regolith study used Arabidopsis, a model plant rather than a food crop, and samples from three Apollo sites [1]. The GreenMOSS figures are design targets [6]. The Chang'e-4 details come largely from secondary news coverage, and the primary technical record was not located.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A lunar agriculture demonstrator would be a surface payload, requiring Earth integration, launch, transfer toward the Moon, landing delivery, deployment on a stable surface, and connection to power, data and thermal interfaces. The Chang'e-4 canister was carried on the lander and operated as part of its payload [2][3]. A greenhouse-class payload would also need stowage, deployment and inflation or pressurisation sequences, as the inflatable-shell concept implies [6]. Its thermal, mechanical and power interfaces would depend on the chosen lander, which has not been identified. Compatibility with any named lander, rover or spacecraft is not asserted, because verified interface evidence was not found. The Apollo 14 seeds travelled in the command module, a crewed spacecraft rather than a surface delivery route [4].
transportation_process: Integrate the payload into a lander or dedicated surface package on Earth.
Launch on a launch vehicle, transfer toward the Moon and land.
Deploy the enclosure on a stable surface and check levelling and thermal protection.
Connect power, data and any water or life-support interfaces.
Begin operations with a controlled start-up, then monitor germination and growth.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Surface deployment method not specified for this payload class. The Chang'e-4 canister was carried on a lander; the GreenMOSS concept assumes an inflatable outer shell around a rigid core.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Chang'e-4 canister travelled on the lander as part of its payload [2][3]. The Apollo 14 seeds travelled in the command module [4].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with any named lander, rover or spacecraft is not asserted. Assessment would require the payload's mass, dimensions, mounting, landing loads, power, thermal and data interfaces to be compared with verified spacecraft specifications.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 14 seed carriage (1971) is the earliest flown example in the sources reviewed of plant material taken to the Moon's vicinity [4]. The Chang'e-4 mini-biosphere was reported as the first plant germination on the Moon, with cotton sprouting in January 2019 before the plants died [2][3]. The Apollo regolith study compared plant growth in actual Apollo samples with a simulant [1]. The GreenMOSS concept reflects ESA's MELiSSA life-support programme [5][6].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The payload name describes a goal rather than a single design, and no flown lunar agriculture demonstrator in the sources reviewed has completed a growth cycle on the Moon. Evidence comes from a short-lived flown canister reported mainly through news coverage, from Earth-based regolith experiments, and from a design study with targets rather than measurements [1][2][3][6]. Reports on which seeds sprouted in the Chang'e-4 canister conflict [2][3]. Values for mass, size and power of the Chang'e-4 canister are unverified. Full-text checks of the regolith paper, the Chang'e-4 technical record and image asset URLs were not completed; this article therefore makes no verified image-asset claims.

data_quality_notes: Chang'e-4 canister mass, size and contents rely on secondary news coverage. Reported figures (18 cm long, about 2.6 kg, roughly six pounds) conflict or are unverified and are recorded as null.
Reports conflict on whether rapeseed and potato seeds also sprouted in the Chang'e-4 canister; only cotton germination is treated as reported by the sources read.
The Chongqing University Chang'e-4 experiment has no peer-reviewed publication located; one news report states the lead designer does not plan to publish papers.

The Paul, Elardo and Ferl 2022 paper was identified through Europe PMC metadata; the full text was not accessible, so sample masses, gene counts and growth statistics beyond the abstract-level summary are not included.
The GreenMOSS cultivation area, edible dry mass and operating duration are design targets from a preliminary design study, not measurements, and no flight or build status is established.
The Apollo 14 seed count is inconsistent within the NASA page ('possibly 2,000 or more seeds' and 'hundreds of tree seeds'); both are reported without reconciliation.
The Goddard Moon Tree image is linked by source page only. Its credit is as reported in a summary of the page and was not checked against the image file.
Several reference entries (3, 5, 6) were cited from search-result summaries and were not fetched in full; they should be checked against the originals before publication.
